topics: The Living World and Biological Classification
Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Which is the basic unit of classification in the taxonomic hierarchy?
questions.explanation: A species is the lowest and basic category of the taxonomic hierarchy; groups of related species form a genus.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: The system of giving each organism a two-part scientific name was introduced by
questions.explanation: Carolus Linnaeus popularised binomial nomenclature, in which a name has a genus part and a species part.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: In the scientific name Mangifera indica Linn., the word 'Linn.' indicates
options: the author who first described the species
the place where the species was found
questions.explanation: The author's name, often abbreviated, is written after the species name; Linn. stands for Linnaeus.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: In the five kingdom classification of Whittaker, unicellular eukaryotic organisms such as Amoeba and Paramecium are placed in kingdom
questions.explanation: Kingdom Protista includes unicellular eukaryotes such as protozoans, diatoms and dinoflagellates.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Which of the following lists the taxonomic categories correctly from the highest to the lowest rank?
options: Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Order, Genus, Family, Species
Phylum, Kingdom, Class, Family, Order, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Phylum, Order, Class, Family, Genus, Species
questions.explanation: The standard hierarchy is Kingdom, Phylum (Division in plants), Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: A microbiologist finds a unicellular organism with no nuclear membrane, 70S ribosomes and a cell wall containing peptidoglycan. It should be placed in kingdom
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes with peptidoglycan cell walls are bacteria, which belong to kingdom Monera.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: State any two rules followed while writing the scientific name of an organism.
questions.answer: The name is in Latin and printed in italics (underlined separately when handwritten); the genus name starts with a capital letter and the species name with a small letter.
keyPoints: Latin names, italicised or underlined separately
Genus name begins with a capital letter
Species name begins with a small letter
questions.explanation: These are the conventions of binomial nomenclature.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Why are viruses not included in the five kingdom classification?
questions.answer: Viruses are non-cellular and show characters of life only inside a host cell, where they multiply as obligate parasites; outside the host they behave like non-living particles, so they do not fit any kingdom.
keyPoints: Obligate parasites that multiply only in host cells
Behave as non-living outside the host
questions.explanation: The five kingdom system classifies cellular organisms only.

questions.q: The pigment that gives brown algae their characteristic colour is
questions.explanation: Brown algae (Phaeophyceae) contain the xanthophyll fucoxanthin in large amounts.

questions.q: Mosses and liverworts belong to the group
questions.explanation: Bryophytes include liverworts and mosses and are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom.

questions.q: In pteridophytes such as ferns, the dominant independent phase of the life cycle is the
questions.explanation: The main plant body of a fern is the diploid sporophyte; the gametophyte is a small prothallus.

questions.q: Gymnosperms are said to have 'naked seeds' because their
options: ovules are not enclosed within an ovary wall
questions.explanation: In gymnosperms the ovules lie exposed on the megasporophylls, so seeds are not enclosed in fruits.

questions.q: A plant has vascular tissues and motile male gametes that need water for fertilisation, but it produces no seeds. It most likely belongs to
questions.explanation: Pteridophytes have xylem and phloem and swimming antherozoids but reproduce by spores, not seeds.

questions.q: In a haplontic life cycle, the only diploid stage is the
questions.explanation: In haplontic algae such as Spirogyra, the zygote undergoes meiosis and the main body is haploid.

questions.q: Distinguish between bryophytes and pteridophytes in terms of the dominant phase of their life cycle.
questions.answer: In bryophytes the dominant phase is the haploid gametophyte, with a dependent sporophyte; in pteridophytes the dominant phase is the independent diploid sporophyte, and the gametophyte is small.
keyPoints: Bryophyte sporophyte depends on the gametophyte
questions.explanation: The change in dominant phase is a major trend in plant evolution.

questions.q: Why do bryophytes remain small and grow in moist places?
questions.answer: They lack true vascular tissues to carry water and food over long distances, and their male gametes swim in water to reach the egg, so they need moist surroundings.
keyPoints: Water needed for fertilisation by swimming gametes
Absorb water directly through the surface
questions.explanation: Absence of conducting tissue limits height, and fertilisation depends on water.

questions.q: Animals with a spiny skin and a water vascular system belong to phylum
questions.explanation: Echinoderms such as starfish and sea urchins have spiny endoskeletons and a water vascular system.

questions.q: Which phylum is acoelomate, having no body cavity?
questions.explanation: Flatworms such as Taenia and Fasciola have a solid body without a coelom.

questions.q: Which of these animals has an open circulatory system?
questions.explanation: Arthropods like the cockroach have an open circulatory system with blood flowing into body spaces.

questions.q: Collar cells called choanocytes line the body cavity of
questions.explanation: Choanocytes with flagella create the water current in sponges (Porifera).

questions.q: A land vertebrate has dry skin covered with scales, lays shelled eggs on land and is cold-blooded. It belongs to class
questions.explanation: Reptiles have scaly dry skin, lay shelled eggs and are poikilothermic.

questions.q: A marine animal shows radial symmetry, tissue-level organisation and stinging cells called cnidoblasts. Its phylum is
questions.explanation: Cnidoblasts (cnidocytes) are characteristic of Cnidaria such as Hydra and jellyfish.

questions.q: Differentiate between diploblastic and triploblastic animals with one example each.
questions.answer: Diploblastic animals have two germ layers, ectoderm and endoderm (e.g. Hydra); triploblastic animals have a third layer, mesoderm, between them (e.g. earthworm or human).
keyPoints: Triploblastic: three germ layers with mesoderm
questions.explanation: The number of germ layers is a basis of animal classification.

questions.q: Explain how birds are adapted for flight.
questions.answer: Birds have forelimbs modified into wings, feathers, a streamlined body and pneumatic bones with air cavities that reduce body weight.
questions.explanation: These features make the body light and suited for flying.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Root hairs are found in the
questions.explanation: Root hairs arise in the zone of maturation and absorb water and minerals.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: The type of venation in the leaves of monocotyledons is generally
questions.explanation: Monocot leaves usually show parallel venation, whereas dicot leaves show reticulate venation.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: The banyan tree supports its heavy branches with
questions.explanation: Prop roots grow down from the branches of the banyan and act as pillars.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: In angiosperm phloem, each sieve tube element is closely associated with a
questions.explanation: Companion cells regulate the functioning of sieve tube elements.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Annual rings in the trunk of a tree growing in a temperate region form because
options: vascular cambium is more active in some seasons than others
phloem is produced only once a year
questions.explanation: Cambium produces large-lumen wood in spring and narrow-lumen wood in autumn, giving visible rings.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Marginal placentation, with ovules along the ventral suture of a single-chambered ovary, is found in
questions.explanation: Pea and other legumes have a monocarpellary ovary with marginal placentation.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Differentiate between a tap root system and a fibrous root system with an example of each.
questions.answer: A tap root system has a main root developed from the radicle with lateral branches, as in mustard (dicots); a fibrous root system has many thin roots arising from the base of the stem, as in wheat (monocots).
keyPoints: Tap root from radicle, e.g. mustard
Fibrous roots from stem base, e.g. wheat
Taproot in dicots, fibrous in monocots
questions.explanation: In monocots the primary root is short lived and replaced by fibrous roots.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Why do dicot stems show secondary growth while monocot stems usually do not?
questions.answer: Dicot stems have open vascular bundles with cambium between xylem and phloem, which divides to add secondary tissues; monocot bundles are closed and lack cambium.
keyPoints: Dicot bundles are open with cambium
Monocot bundles are closed without cambium
Cambium produces secondary xylem and phloem
questions.explanation: Presence of cambium makes secondary thickening possible.

questions.q: The tissue that lines the cavities of the body and forms the covering of organs is
questions.explanation: Epithelial tissue forms the covering or lining of body surfaces and cavities.

questions.q: Intercalated discs are a feature of
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle cells are joined by intercalated discs with gap junctions for rapid communication.

questions.q: The abdomen of a cockroach is made up of how many segments?
questions.explanation: The cockroach abdomen has ten segments in both sexes.

questions.q: The blood-like fluid that fills the body cavity of a cockroach is called
questions.explanation: Cockroach blood is haemolymph, which is colourless and lacks respiratory pigment.

questions.q: In the frog, mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood takes place mainly in the
questions.explanation: The frog has a three-chambered heart with a single ventricle, so blood mixes there.

questions.q: Dense regular connective tissue that attaches a skeletal muscle to a bone is called a
questions.explanation: Tendons attach muscle to bone; ligaments attach bone to bone.

questions.q: Name the three types of cell junctions found in animal tissues and state the function of each.
questions.answer: Tight junctions prevent leakage of substances across a tissue; adhering junctions cement neighbouring cells together; gap junctions connect the cytoplasm of adjoining cells to allow transfer of ions and small molecules.
questions.explanation: Junctions are found especially in epithelial and other tissues.

questions.q: Why is the vision of a cockroach described as mosaic vision?
questions.answer: Each compound eye has about 2000 hexagonal ommatidia, and each forms a separate image part, so the image is a mosaic; it gives more sensitivity but less resolution.
keyPoints: Each ommatidium forms a part of the image
Gives mosaic image, more sensitivity but less resolution
questions.explanation: Vision with many ommatidia is called mosaic vision.

questions.q: Which cell organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria produce most of the cell's ATP through aerobic respiration.

questions.q: The fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane was proposed by
questions.explanation: Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model in 1972.

questions.q: The ribosomes of prokaryotic cells have a sedimentation coefficient of
questions.explanation: Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, made of 50S and 30S subunits.

questions.q: The site of synthesis of ribosomal RNA and assembly of ribosome subunits in the nucleus is the
questions.explanation: The nucleolus is a non-membrane-bound region rich in rRNA and protein.

questions.q: A drug stops the functioning of the Golgi apparatus in a gland cell. Which process would be affected most directly?
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus modifies, packages and dispatches proteins and lipids for secretion.

questions.q: Which pair of organelles contains its own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are semi-autonomous organelles.

questions.q: Write any three differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
questions.answer: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles, have 70S ribosomes and a single circular DNA; eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus, membrane-bound organelles and 80S ribosomes.
questions.explanation: These are the main structural differences.

questions.q: Pancreatic acinar cells that secrete digestive enzymes are rich in rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi bodies. Explain why.
questions.answer: Digestive enzymes are proteins made by ribosomes on the RER, which folds and transports them; the Golgi then modifies, packs and secretes them, so cells that secrete much protein need large amounts of both.
keyPoints: Heavy secretion needs more of both
questions.explanation: Organelle abundance matches the cell's function.

questions.q: The monomers of proteins are
questions.explanation: Proteins are polymers of amino acids.

questions.q: Two amino acids are joined together by a
questions.explanation: A peptide bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next.

questions.q: Enzymes increase the rate of a reaction by
options: being used up in the reaction
questions.explanation: Enzymes lower the energy barrier and are not consumed.

questions.q: Malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase because it
questions.explanation: Malonate is a competitive inhibitor that competes with succinate for the active site.

questions.q: An enzyme has a Vmax of 100 units. At a substrate concentration equal to its Km, the reaction velocity will be
questions.explanation: Km is the substrate concentration at which the velocity is half of Vmax.

questions.q: Humans cannot digest cellulose even though it is a polymer of glucose, because they lack an enzyme that
questions.explanation: Cellulose has beta 1-4 linkages, unlike starch which has alpha linkages digestible by amylase.

questions.q: Briefly describe the primary, secondary and tertiary structures of a protein.
questions.answer: Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids; secondary structure is the regular folding into alpha helix or beta pleated sheet; tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the chain.
questions.explanation: A fourth level, quaternary, arises when several chains join.

questions.q: Why can the effect of a competitive inhibitor be reduced by adding more substrate?
questions.answer: The inhibitor and substrate compete for the same active site; at a high substrate concentration the substrate outnumbers the inhibitor and occupies most active sites, so the inhibition is overcome.
keyPoints: Both bind the same active site
questions.explanation: This is the characteristic of competitive inhibition.

questions.q: DNA replication takes place in the
questions.explanation: DNA is duplicated during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase.

questions.q: Synapsis, the pairing of homologous chromosomes, occurs during
questions.explanation: In zygotene of prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair to form bivalents.

questions.q: Crossing over takes place during which sub-stage of meiotic prophase I?
questions.explanation: Recombination nodules appear and crossing over occurs in pachytene.

questions.q: A cell with 20 chromosomes (2n = 20) undergoes meiosis. How many chromosomes does each cell have at the end of meiosis I?
questions.explanation: Meiosis I is reductional, so each daughter cell has n = 10 chromosomes.

questions.q: A plant cell has 2n = 14. How many chromatids are present at metaphase of mitosis?
questions.explanation: At metaphase there are 14 chromosomes, each with two chromatids, giving 28.

questions.q: Which event in meiosis most directly increases genetic variation?
options: Exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
Duplication of DNA in S phase
questions.explanation: Crossing over and independent assortment produce new gene combinations.

questions.q: What is cytokinesis? How does it differ in plant and animal cells?
questions.answer: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm after karyokinesis. Animal cells form a cleavage furrow that pinches the cell, while plant cells form a cell plate in the centre that grows outward.
questions.explanation: The rigid wall of plant cells requires a cell plate.

questions.q: Why is meiosis essential in sexually reproducing organisms?
questions.answer: It halves the chromosome number in gametes so that fertilisation restores the diploid number, keeping it constant across generations, and it creates variation through crossing over.
questions.explanation: Without meiosis the chromosome number would double every generation.

questions.q: The main pigment that takes part directly in the light reaction of photosynthesis is
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll a is the primary pigment; the others are accessory pigments.

questions.q: The dark (biosynthetic) reaction of photosynthesis takes place in the
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma of the chloroplast.

questions.q: The first stable product of CO2 fixation in C3 plants is
questions.explanation: RuBisCO fixes CO2 to RuBP to form two molecules of 3-PGA.

questions.q: The most abundant enzyme on Earth, which catalyses both carboxylation and oxygenation, is
questions.explanation: RuBisCO acts as a carboxylase in the Calvin cycle and as an oxygenase in photorespiration.

questions.q: In C4 plants the primary fixation of CO2 in mesophyll cells is catalysed by
questions.explanation: PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 to PEP forming oxaloacetic acid, a four-carbon compound.

questions.q: Photorespiration is negligible in C4 plants because
options: CO2 is concentrated around RuBisCO in bundle sheath cells
questions.explanation: Concentrated CO2 prevents RuBisCO from acting as an oxygenase.

questions.q: What are the products of the light reaction and where does the oxygen come from?
questions.answer: The light reaction yields ATP and NADPH; the oxygen released comes from the splitting (photolysis) of water, not from CO2.
questions.explanation: Water splitting is associated with photosystem II.

questions.q: Compare cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
questions.answer: Non-cyclic involves both PS II and PS I, gives ATP, NADPH and O2; cyclic involves only PS I, electrons return to it, and only ATP is made, with no NADPH or oxygen.
keyPoints: Non-cyclic: PS I and PS II, ATP + NADPH + O2
Cyclic: PS I only, ATP only
questions.explanation: Cyclic flow occurs in the stroma lamellae.

questions.q: Glycolysis takes place in the
questions.explanation: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm of all living cells.

questions.q: The end product of glycolysis is
questions.explanation: One glucose molecule is broken down into two molecules of pyruvic acid.

questions.q: The net gain of ATP molecules from glycolysis of one glucose molecule is
questions.explanation: Four ATP are produced and two are consumed, giving a net gain of two.

questions.q: The final acceptor of electrons in the mitochondrial electron transport chain is
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c oxidase passes electrons to oxygen, forming water.

questions.q: The respiratory quotient (RQ) when fats are the respiratory substrate is generally
questions.explanation: Fats contain less oxygen than carbohydrates, so more oxygen is consumed than CO2 released; for tripalmitin RQ is about 0.7.

questions.q: When yeast ferments glucose in the absence of oxygen, pyruvic acid is converted into
questions.explanation: Alcoholic fermentation yields ethanol and CO2.

questions.q: Differentiate between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
questions.answer: Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and completely oxidises glucose to CO2 and water, releasing much energy; anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen, gives incomplete oxidation (alcohol or lactic acid) and releases little energy.
questions.explanation: Fermentation is the anaerobic route in yeast.

questions.q: Why is the energy yield of fermentation much lower than that of aerobic respiration?
questions.answer: In fermentation glucose is only partially broken down and the electron transport chain is not used, so only 2 ATP are made by glycolysis, while aerobic respiration oxidises pyruvate fully and gains many more ATP through oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.explanation: Most ATP comes from the electron transport chain.

questions.q: The plant hormone that promotes apical dominance and cell elongation is
questions.explanation: Auxins such as IAA are produced at the shoot tip and cause cell elongation and apical dominance.

questions.q: The gaseous hormone that promotes fruit ripening is
questions.explanation: Ethylene hastens ripening of fruits such as tomato and banana.

questions.q: Bolting, the sudden elongation of the internodes in rosette plants like cabbage, is caused by
questions.explanation: Gibberellins promote internode elongation and bolting before flowering.

questions.q: Which hormone promotes cell division and delays senescence of leaves?
questions.explanation: Cytokinins, first isolated as kinetin, stimulate cytokinesis and delay leaf ageing.

questions.q: During a drought, closure of stomata to reduce water loss is mainly brought about by
questions.explanation: ABA is the stress hormone that causes stomatal closure.

questions.q: Winter varieties of wheat flower in the following summer only after exposure to cold. This process is called
questions.explanation: Vernalisation is the promotion of flowering by exposure to low temperature.

questions.q: Name the three phases of growth in a plant cell and state what happens in each.
questions.answer: Meristematic phase: cells divide actively. Elongation phase: cells enlarge with vacuolation and new wall deposition. Maturation phase: cells attain their final size and structure and differentiate.
questions.explanation: These phases are seen in root and shoot apices.

questions.q: Explain how removing the shoot tip of a plant makes it grow more side branches.
questions.answer: The shoot tip makes auxin that moves down and inhibits growth of axillary buds (apical dominance). Removing the tip removes this auxin, so the lateral buds grow into branches.
questions.explanation: Gardeners prune hedges to make them bushy for this reason.

questions.q: The enzyme present in saliva that starts digestion of starch is
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase breaks starch into maltose in the buccal cavity.

questions.q: Most of the absorption of digested food takes place in the
questions.explanation: The small intestine, with villi, is the main site of absorption.

questions.q: Bile, which helps in the emulsification of fats, is produced by the
questions.explanation: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

questions.q: The major portion of carbon dioxide in blood is transported as
questions.explanation: About 70 per cent of CO2 is carried as bicarbonate in the plasma.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of conduction of the cardiac impulse?
options: SA node, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres
AV node, SA node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres
SA node, Purkinje fibres, bundle of His, AV node
Bundle of His, SA node, AV node, Purkinje fibres
questions.explanation: The SA node is the pacemaker; the impulse passes to the AV node, the bundle of His and then Purkinje fibres.

questions.q: A person has a tidal volume of 500 mL, inspiratory reserve volume of 3000 mL and expiratory reserve volume of 1100 mL. The vital capacity is
questions.explanation: Vital capacity = TV + IRV + ERV = 500 + 3000 + 1100 = 4600 mL.

questions.q: State the role of HCl and pepsinogen in the stomach.
questions.answer: HCl provides an acidic medium (pH about 1.8), kills microbes and converts inactive pepsinogen into active pepsin; pepsin then breaks proteins into proteoses and peptones.
keyPoints: HCl gives acid pH and kills germs
questions.explanation: Gastric glands secrete both, and mucus protects the stomach wall.

questions.q: Explain why haemoglobin releases more oxygen in actively respiring tissues.
questions.answer: Tissues have a high pCO2, high H+ concentration (low pH) and higher temperature, and these lower the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen, shifting the dissociation curve to the right so more oxygen is released.
keyPoints: High pCO2 and H+, lower pH, higher temperature
Reduced affinity of haemoglobin for O2
Curve shifts to right, more O2 released
questions.explanation: This is the Bohr effect.

questions.q: The functional unit of the kidney is the
questions.explanation: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons.

questions.q: The hormone that increases water reabsorption in the distal parts of the nephron is
questions.explanation: ADH released from the neurohypophysis prevents loss of water in urine.

questions.q: The sodium-potassium pump of a neuron maintains the resting potential by moving
questions.explanation: The pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in per cycle.

questions.q: During muscle contraction, calcium ions bind to
questions.explanation: Ca2+ binds troponin, exposing myosin-binding sites on actin.

questions.q: A person feels constant thirst, passes a large volume of urine and has glucose in the urine, because of too little insulin action. The condition is
questions.explanation: Lack of insulin raises blood glucose; excess glucose spills into urine (glycosuria).

questions.q: In a healthy adult the glomerular filtration rate is about
questions.explanation: GFR is about 125 mL per minute, i.e. about 180 litres a day.

questions.q: Describe the path of a reflex arc.
questions.answer: A stimulus excites a receptor; the sensory (afferent) neuron carries the impulse to the spinal cord, where it is passed to a motor (efferent) neuron, often via an interneuron, which takes it to the effector, producing the response.
questions.explanation: A reflex is an involuntary rapid response.

questions.q: Explain how the renin-angiotensin mechanism raises blood pressure when the glomerular filtration falls.
questions.answer: A fall in GFR makes the juxtaglomerular cells release renin, which leads to formation of angiotensin II; this narrows blood vessels and stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, causing Na+ and water reabsorption, which restores blood volume and pressure.
keyPoints: Aldosterone increases Na+ and water reabsorption
questions.explanation: This restores GFR.
